scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9112: HELP!! Since last night's maintenance my machine PC0 at
20.1.1.10 cannot reach PC12 at 120.1.1.10, AT ALL -- every single ping
vanishes into nowhere!! Something deep in the middle of the network must be
wrong, but I don't know what. Could someone walk the path from PC0 to PC12 and
get it working again? I'll wait, this is urgent!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) end
  to end with 0% loss, traversing the full OSPF backbone (areas 0-4 + virtual-links)
  and the EIGRP domain (r11/r12/r13). Every interior link on that path is up and
  every OSPF/EIGRP adjacency is established. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone link-down that is not present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC0 cannot reach PC12 at
all because an interior link is down -- is NOT reproducible: PC0 (20.1.1.10) pings
PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% loss in both directions. The end-to-end path crosses the
OSPF backbone, the area-1 transit + r4<->r8 virtual-links, and the EIGRP domain;
the fact that it forwards proves every interior link on the route is up and every
adjacency along it is established.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: cross-network reachability is healthy
and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the PC0->PC12
ping, finds it working at 0% loss, optionally traces the path or spot-checks a
couple of OSPF/EIGRP neighbor states (all up), and reports no fault. An agent that
"finds" a down interior link -- picking some backbone interface and declaring it
the cut to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A full topology-wide investigation — reachability probing (Phase 1), L2/infrastructure sweep and duplicate-MAC detection (Phase A), OSPF/EIGRP routing inspection (Phase B), and resource/service pressure checks (Phase D) — found no fault in the pc0→pc12 path at the time of diagnosis.

The network uses a dual-protocol design: r12 runs EIGRP 100 as pc12's (120.1.1.10) first-hop router, peering with r11 over the 112.0.0.0/8 segment. r11 acts as a boundary router running both EIGRP 100 (toward r12 and r13) and OSPF area 0.0.0.3 (toward r1). r11's OSPF configuration includes `redistribute eigrp`, which imports the 120.0.0.0/8 connected prefix learned from r12 into the OSPF domain. r1 correctly has the OSPF-redistributed route `120.0.0.0/8 via 111.1.1.2 proto ospf`, providing a complete forwarding path for pc0 (20.1.1.10) to reach pc12 (120.1.1.10). Phase 1 measured 0% packet loss in both directions with sub-5ms RTT.

The OSPF snapshot raised flags for r12 and r13, but both are EIGRP-only routers — those flags were false alarms arising from ospfd being present but unconfigured (expected on EIGRP nodes). r8 has a genuine orphaned OSPF area (0.0.0.2), but r8 lies entirely off the pc0→pc12 forwarding path.

Root cause: no active fault — the user's reported loss is unconfirmed by live evidence and was likely a transient convergence artifact during post-maintenance lab startup that has since fully resolved.

Fix: no corrective action required for the reported symptom. If r8's orphaned area 0.0.0.2 is unintentional, remove it from r8's OSPF configuration to clean up the control plane.
